**The two arms.** Each was built with `--silu-sigmoid` in its own process, kernel cache and
fresh directory:
- **main:** `main` `fa2db0e`'s own compiler and `engine.cc`, linking a 21,628 B object;
- **merged:** merge `714943f`, which has `ptr` and the dispatch gate, linking a 13,608 B object.

Both Ignition arms run through the merged runtime, so they differ by container.

**Correctness.** The merged YOLOv8s, with workspace reuse off, reads **66/66 layers exact**
against `silu_sigmoid.reference_model` ([log](../results/aie/b3_verify_yolov8s_merged_silu_noreuse_desktop2_20261013T015553Z.log)).

**Latency.** `tools/bench_layout_ab.py`: AMD, main, then merged, twice. Each run is 50 warm-up
frames plus 500 timed on `bus.jpg`, glass-to-glass. It was wrapped in `research-lowlevel.sh
--npu` (`timing_eligible: true`) and saw no foreign context.

| model | arm | round 1 | round 2 | dispatch (r1 / r2) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| YOLOv8s | AMD | **17.071** | **17.047** | `session.run` 13.133 / 13.161 |
| YOLOv8s | main | 17.853 | 17.844 | 16.979 / 16.955 |
| YOLOv8s | merged | 17.199 | 17.194 | 16.305 / 16.299 |
| YOLOv8n | AMD | 10.727 | 10.790 | `session.run` 6.904 / 6.953 |
| YOLOv8n | main | 8.390 | 8.445 | 7.522 / 7.572 |
| YOLOv8n | merged | **8.199** | **8.163** | 7.314 / 7.290 |

- **W (YOLOv8s beats AMD in both rounds): FAILS.** Merged is 0.128 and 0.147 ms slower than AMD,
  about 0.8%. With the shipped recipe, AMD keeps YOLOv8s.
- **R (YOLOv8n no slower than main): PASSES.** Merged is 0.191 and 0.282 ms faster.
- **Reported, not gated:** merged is 0.654 and 0.650 ms faster than main on YOLOv8s (-3.7%),
  close to the 2026-09-22 control-to-`ptr` delta (-4.4%, -4.3%) without the flag.

**Where the gap is.** AMD's `session.run` (13.13 ms) is 3.2 ms faster than the merged
dispatch (16.31 ms). Ignition wins most of that back on the host:
- 0.31 ms of preprocess against AMD's 1.87 ms letterbox;
- 0.17 ms of fused decode against AMD's 2.07 ms.

So the remaining YOLOv8s lever is NPU time, the instruction-stream bound named in this branch's
cost model, not host work.

**Scope.** One image, one sitting, glass-to-glass; no energy, no accuracy rescore (the flag's
accuracy is measured in its own section). Logs:
- the A/B wrappers [b3_ab_yolov8s_silu_desktop2_20261013T015609Z.log](../results/aie/b3_ab_yolov8s_silu_desktop2_20261013T015609Z.log) and [b3_ab_yolov8n_silu_desktop2_20261013T015752Z.log](../results/aie/b3_ab_yolov8n_silu_desktop2_20261013T015752Z.log);
- the tool's own logs [b3_ab_yolov8s_phoenix_20261013T0156Z.log](../results/aie/b3_ab_yolov8s_phoenix_20261013T0156Z.log) and [b3_ab_yolov8n_phoenix_20261013T0157Z.log](../results/aie/b3_ab_yolov8n_phoenix_20261013T0157Z.log).

## What AMD's compiled YOLOv8 runs: its control barely grows while its work doubles (2026-10-13, Desktop 2)

**Question.** With the shipped recipe, AMD keeps YOLOv8s:
- AMD's `session.run` takes 13.13-13.16 ms;
- the merged engine's dispatch takes 16.30-16.31 ms
  ([above](#with-the-shipped-silu-recipe-ptr-does-not-carry-yolov8s-past-amds-stack-1720-against-1706-ms-2026-10-13-desktop-2)).

What does AMD's stack do on the device that ours does not? This reads the artifacts AMD's
compiler left from that sitting. Nothing was modified, and nothing modified was run.

**Pre-registered** (scratch, sha256 `9688c826...`), before any AMD instruction-buffer size was read:
- At the engine's own prices
  ([cost model](#what-a-whole-frame-is-bound-by-the-instruction-stream-not-the-bytes-and-not-the-loop-derived-2026-09-22)),
  3.2 ms is about 200 KB of instruction stream.
- **H-count:** AMD's per-frame instruction (CODE) buffer is at least 200 KB smaller than our
  969,812 B, so "fewer packets" is the gap.
- **H-model:** AMD's CODE buffer is comparable or larger, so the gap is in the execution model.
- **Between:** neither clearly holds.
- AMD's bytes are reported as sizes only; our 16 ns per byte is not applied to them.

**Where AMD's 13.13 ms goes.** The EP report places 922 of 929 nodes in one DPU subgraph. The 7 on
CPU are the input `QuantizeLinear` (1x3x640x640 float) and the six output `DequantizeLinear`s.
Both sit inside `session.run`, so AMD's on-device time is below 13.13 ms. The on-device gap is
therefore at least 3.2 ms.

**What each compiler declares.** `tools/amd_xmodel_census.py` reads the compiled `.xmodel` (an XIR
protobuf) without a vendor library, alongside the engine containers' manifests from the same
sitting. Every row is a static declaration, not a measurement.

| | AMD YOLOv8n | AMD YOLOv8s | engine YOLOv8n | engine YOLOv8s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `mc_code` / instruction stream | 93,840 B | 106,168 B | 419,476 B | 969,812 B |
| CODE register (REG_4) | 1,473,536 B | 1,593,408 B | - | - |
| `0x0B`-headed words in `mc_code` | 1,520 | 1,757 | - | - |
| activation reads | 69.4 MB | 138.1 MB | 83.1 MB | 237.7 MB |
| activation writes | 44.8 MB | 73.0 MB | 15.3 MB (DERIVED) | 27.7 MB (DERIVED) |
| weight reads | 26.2 MB (8.0x REG_0) | 87.9 MB (7.5x REG_0) | 8.2 MB | 29.5 MB |
| **total** | **140.4 MB** | **299.0 MB** | **106.5 MB** | **294.9 MB** |
| workload (`workload_on_arch`) | 11.97 G | 38.99 G | - | - |
| NPU time (sitting above) | 6.90 / 6.95 `session.run` | 13.13 / 13.16 `session.run` | 7.31 / 7.29 dispatch | 16.31 / 16.30 dispatch |

Sources:
- **AMD:** the activation and weight rows are its own `input_feature_load_size`,
  `output_feature_save_size` and `const_data_load_size`.
- **Engine reads:** its 6,400 B activation packets. The compiler counts input fills only;
  drains are scheduled separately (`compiler/engine_schedule.py`). Weights are `wpackets_bytes`.
- **Engine writes:** DERIVED, each layer's output written once (interior H x W x C).
- **Buffer dump:** AMD's own runner (`XLNX_ENABLE_DUMP_BO=1`, unmodified xmodel) confirms the
  three data registers byte for byte: input 1,638,400, workspace 40,576,896, output 1,209,792. It
  writes no instruction buffer, so neither candidate program buffer was observed at run time.

**Verdict on the size test: Between.** The pre-registered criterion depends on which buffer counts
as AMD's program:
- `mc_code`, at 106 KB, is 864 KB smaller than our stream, which reads H-count;
- the CODE register, at 1.59 MB, is larger, which reads H-model.

**What does not depend on that choice is scaling.** From YOLOv8n to YOLOv8s:
- AMD's control grows 13% (`mc_code`) or 8% (CODE);
- its declared bytes grow 2.13x, its workload 3.26x and its `session.run` 1.90x;
- our instruction stream grows 2.31x and our dispatch 2.23x, matching the cost model's ~16 ns per
  instruction byte on these containers too.

So the measured claim is a negative one: **AMD's frame time is insensitive to the size of its
control program, and ours is not.** What AMD's time does follow, bytes or compute, cannot be
separated from two models, because both grow together.

`mc_code` is a stream of records. Many begin with a `0x0B0000xx` word, 48 bytes apart on YOLOv8s,
and about 1.8k of them describe a frame. No field meaning is claimed for any record; 1,551 words per
model are printable ASCII. The per-frame program does not unroll with the work, whoever expands it.

**Bytes are not where AMD wins.** The two YOLOv8s frames declare nearly the same traffic, 299.0 MB
against the engine's 294.9 MB. The engine moves 1.7x the activation reads; AMD moves 3.0x the
weights and 2.6x the writes. The implied rates differ: AMD's is at least 22.8 GB/s (`session.run`
includes the CPU QDQ), the engine's 18.1 GB/s. At equal rates the two frames would take about the
same time. This is DERIVED and not a latency prediction.

> **Basis caveat, found 2026-10-13** ([below](#what-the-cost-model-tiler-changes-and-where-its-23-ms-comes-from-2026-10-13-desktop-2)). AMD's subgraph-level byte fields, which
> this table uses, are exactly 2x the sum of its per-layer records. This holds in all four xmodels
> checked (YOLOv8s and YOLOv8n, default and cost-model tiling), while the op counts agree 1x. Which
> level is per frame is not established. If the per-layer sum is, AMD's YOLOv8s declares 149.5 MB,
> the engine moves about twice AMD's bytes, and the paragraph above does not hold. The figures
> stand as declared; only their per-frame reading is in question.

**What this says to build.**
- **Not coarser shim tasks.** That lever is spent: the coarse schedule already merges fills and
  repeats weight runs (`docs/DECISIONS.md`, 2,972 tasks per frame). YOLOv8s's fill tasks sit at
  their structural floor, 37,136 packets in 5,857 tasks
  ([2026-09-16](#memtile-residency-does-not-pay-on-the-graph-engine-and-the-yolov8s-gap-is-a-known-limitation-2026-09-16-desktop-2)).
  The shim's repeat dimension also caps at 64.
- **The open lever is a control stream that does not unroll per round,** as AMD's does not. Two
  routes; neither is sized yet:
  - a looping or resident schedule;
  - fewer rounds, through less activation re-fetch: the "fewer packets" lever in the cost-model
    section.
- **Unexplained:** how AMD's 48-byte commands become transfers, and whether its cores or the
  shim's command processor drive them. That is the next read-only question for the RE tools.

**AMD's compile options, as recorded** (`--root-attrs`, 119 per model). These include:
- `tiling_algorithm = "high_throughput"`;
- `prefetch_lp = 8`, `prefetch_lp_warm_start = 1`, `prefetch_lp_reorder_load = 1`;
- `enable_control_optimization = 1`, `mergesync_column_as_all = 1`, `enable_ddr_memory_planner = 1`.

Off in this build: `enable_weights_prefetch`, `enable_ifm_stationary`, `enable_weights_stationary`
and `enable_cost_model_tiling`. Whether any of those makes AMD's own stack faster is untested.

**Scope.** Two models, one sitting's artifacts, static declarations. The xmodels match that
sitting by mtime (01:56Z and 01:58Z). Logs:
- the census [amd_xmodel_census_yolov8n_s_desktop2_20261013T021744Z.log](../results/aie/amd_xmodel_census_yolov8n_s_desktop2_20261013T021744Z.log);
- the census with the root attributes and the derived writes
  [amd_xmodel_census_root_yolov8n_s_desktop2_20261013T022314Z.log](../results/aie/amd_xmodel_census_root_yolov8n_s_desktop2_20261013T022314Z.log);
- the dump run [amd_yolov8s_bo_dump_desktop2_20261013T021506Z.log](../results/aie/amd_yolov8s_bo_dump_desktop2_20261013T021506Z.log),
  whose 46 ms frames carry the dump's own cost and are not a timing, and its file list
  [amd_yolov8s_bo_dump_sizes_desktop2_20261013T021506Z.log](../results/aie/amd_yolov8s_bo_dump_sizes_desktop2_20261013T021506Z.log).

## How AMD's overlay moves data and control: cores program their own DMAs, and a DDR stream reaches every tile's control port (2026-10-13, Desktop 2)

**Question.** The [census above](#what-amds-compiled-yolov8-runs-its-control-barely-grows-while-its-work-doubles-2026-10-13-desktop-2)
found that AMD's control program barely grows with the model, while the engine's grows with every
round. How do AMD's commands become transfers, and who programs the DMAs?

**Method.** This is read-only and static. `tools/overlay_dataflow_census.py` reads:
- the 15 PDIs of the Phoenix DPU overlay (`phoenix\4x4.xclbin`), extracted by
  `tools/xclbin_overlay_extract.py` on branch `dpu-isa-re`;
- Peano's disassembly of their 240 core images.

Register names and field layouts come from aie-rt's `xaiemlgbl_params.h` and `xaie_ss.c` (SPEC).
The log carries counts and decoded register values only. The AMD binaries stay uncommitted.

**1. The cores program and start their own tiles' DMAs** (decoded from the binaries).
- **`st.tm` is common.** It appears 14,208 times across the 240 images, and in every one of
  them. Lock operations are just as general: 832 `acq`, 1,360 `acq.cond`, 768 `rel` and 1,056
  `rel.cond`.
- **The addresses are tile registers.** Read as `0x80000 + offset`, the immediates feeding those
  stores name memory-module registers. The `0x80000` base is SPEC (Peano): `aiev2intrin.h`
  defines `write_tm(regVal, regAddr, TMAddrSpaceStart = 0x80000)`.
- **Which registers:**
  - `DMA_S2MM_0_START_QUEUE` 560;
  - `LOCK0_VALUE` 256;
  - `DMA_S2MM_1_CTRL` 240;
  - `LOCK14_VALUE` 240;
  - `LOCK12_VALUE` 208;
  - `DMA_BD7_0` 208;
  - `DMA_BD3_4` 208;
  - `LOCK10_VALUE` 64;
  - `LOCK8_VALUE` 16.
- **What this establishes:** each core writes BDs into its own tile's DMA, pushes them onto the
  start queue and manages its locks, with no host instruction per transfer.
- **Coverage:** 2,000 of the 12,129 immediates in the 0x10000–0xFFFFF range resolve this
  way. The bare base `0x80000` is excluded; the rest are not tile registers.

**2. The PDI routes a DDR stream into every tile's control port** (decoded; identical in all 15
PDIs).
- **The routing:**
  - every core, MemTile and shim configures `MASTER_CONFIG_TILE_CTRL`;
  - no PDI writes a single DMA buffer descriptor on any tile;
  - the shim mux sets `SOUTH3` and `SOUTH7` to 1, which aie-rt names
    `XAIE_MUX_DEMUX_CONFIG_TYPE_DMA`, so both ports are fed by the shim's DMA reading DDR.
- **Column 0 of the YOLOv8s PDI**, slots decoded as (id, msel, arbiter) against masters packed as
  `msel_enable << 3 | arbiter` (aie-rt):

  | from | packet ID | to |
  |---|---|---|
  | shim `SOUTH_3` (DDR) | 1 | shim `TILE_CTRL` |
  | shim `SOUTH_3` (DDR) | 2 | MemTile `TILE_CTRL` |
  | shim `SOUTH_3` (DDR) | 3 | `NORTH4` up the column: each core's `SOUTH_4`, which is circuit-routed to both that core's `TILE_CTRL` and the core above |
  | shim `SOUTH_3` (DDR) | 0 | MemTile `DMA0` (S2MM), header dropped |
  | MemTile `DMA_4` (MM2S) | 0 | `NORTH5` up the column: each core's `DMA1` (S2MM), header dropped |
  | MemTile `DMA_4` (MM2S) | 1 | `SOUTH3` toward the shim, header dropped |
  | shim `SOUTH_7` (DDR) | circuit | `NORTH5` |

- **What this establishes:** a single DDR-fed shim DMA stream can write registers in the shim,
  the MemTile and the cores, selected by packet ID. The cores' path is a broadcast: all four
  cores in a column receive identical packets on `TILE_CTRL`, with no per-core addressing.
- **mlir-aie supports this mechanism** upstream (`test/npu-xrt/ctrl_packet_reconfig*`,
  `add_one_ctrl_packet*`). The engine has never used it: no file in `src/`, `kernels/` or
  `tools/` mentions control packets.

**What this does not establish.** Points 1 and 2 are two mechanisms, and neither shows what runs
per frame.
- **What fills the CODE register (REG_4, 1.59 MB) and who consumes it is unobserved.** The
  shim's DDR-side stream into the control ports could carry it. The firmware's command processor
  could equally write shim and MemTile BDs from the `instruct` buffer, with the control-port path
  used only for part of the work (`enable_pad_control_packet = 1` names padding, not more). The
  PDI's lack of static BDs fits both.
- **One DERIVED bound.** At the engine's ~16 ns per instruction byte, 1.59 MB of transaction
  would take about 25 ms, more than AMD's whole frame. So the CODE register is not consumed the
  way the engine's stream is, whatever it holds.
- **Unreconciled packet size:** the RE branch reads 40-byte instruction packets in the core
  programs; the census finds 48-byte strides between `0x0B`-headed `mc_code` words.
- **Which overlay ran:** these PDIs come from the installed `phoenix\4x4.xclbin`. The RE branch
  found that the xclbin embedded in an xmodel differs from that file, so the run-time overlay's
  routing is TO VERIFY. The 15 PDIs here agree with each other.
- **Not priced.** No speedup or per-write cost is claimed for control packets.

**What it says to measure next (Block 5, not run).** On Phoenix, in one sitting, time N register
writes delivered as control packets from a DDR buffer through a shim DMA against the same N
writes as `npu.write32` transaction ops. Use mlir-aie's own `ctrl_packet_reconfig` design (our
artifact, not AMD's), with an exactness check on the written registers. If control packets cost
much less than ~145 ns per write, the engine's per-round BD reprogramming has a cheaper channel.
The control-stream lever named in the census above then has a concrete form.

Log: [overlay_dataflow_census_phoenix4x4_desktop2_20261013T024655Z.log](../results/aie/overlay_dataflow_census_phoenix4x4_desktop2_20261013T024655Z.log).

## Control packets are not a cheaper write channel on Phoenix: the cost is per packet, and packing 4 words buys 3x (2026-10-13, Desktop 2)

**Question.** AMD's overlay routes a DDR stream into every tile's control port
([above](#how-amds-overlay-moves-data-and-control-cores-program-their-own-dmas-and-a-ddr-stream-reaches-every-tiles-control-port-2026-10-13-desktop-2)).
Is a register write cheaper sent as a control packet than as an `npu.write32` op in the
instruction stream? If so, the engine's per-round BD reprogramming would have a cheaper channel.

**Design** (`kernels/ctrl_packet_probe/`, ours, not AMD's).
- **What it writes:** N words into tile (0,2)'s data memory, cycling over a 1,024-word buffer,
  then a lock release. The tile's DMA then streams the buffer to DDR, so every run is checked
  exactly against the expected words.
- **Arms:**
  - `write32`: N ops in the instruction stream.
  - Control packets of 1 or 4 words, each its own stream packet: the shim BD's repeat dimension,
    at most 64 packets per task, then a `dma_wait`.
- **Routing:** aiecc's `--generate-ctrl-pkt-overlay` routes shim MM2S 0, packet ID 27, to the
  tile's `TileControl`. The header layout is from mlir-aie's `add_one_ctrl_packet_col_overlay`
  test.

**Pre-registered** (scratch, sha256 `ee7aed0c...` with its amendment), before any timed run:
- the metric is the least-squares slope, in ns per written word, of the median dispatch time
  over N ∈ {64, 256, 1024, 4096, 16384};
- each (arm, N) runs in its own process: 20 warm-up, 200 timed runs, and an exactness check
  before and after;
- the sweep runs forward, then in reverse;
- **H1:** the 4-word arm's slope is at most 0.2x `write32`'s in both orders;
- **H0:** it is at least 0.5x in either order.

| N | `write32` ms | 1-word packets ms | 4-word packets ms | `write32` insts B | 4-word insts B |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 | 0.1416 / 0.1418 | 0.1439 / 0.1449 | 0.1414 / 0.1441 | 1,764 | 532 |
| 256 | 0.1514 / 0.1506 | 0.1581 / 0.1592 | 0.1440 / 0.1450 | 6,372 | 532 |
| 1,024 | 0.2083 / 0.2070 | 0.2362 / 0.2315 | 0.1577 / 0.1590 | 24,804 | 1,024 |
| 4,096 | 0.4408 / 0.4424 | 0.5263 / 0.5221 | 0.2379 / 0.2374 | 98,532 | 2,992 |
| 16,384 | 1.3285 / 1.3373 | 1.6572 / 1.6200 | 0.5372 / 0.5446 | 393,444 | 10,864 |
| **slope, ns/word** | **72.9 / 73.5** | **92.7 / 90.4** | **24.4 / 24.8** | | |

Each cell gives median dispatch time, forward / reverse. All 30 runs are exact, first and last.
The sweep was `timing_eligible: true` with no foreign process on the NPU.

**Verdict: Between.** The 4-word arm runs at 0.335x / 0.337x `write32`, inside neither line.

**What the numbers say** (MEASURED):
- **Control packets are not cheaper per write.** A 1-word packet costs 90-93 ns, more than a
  `write32` op at 73 ns.
- **Packing pays.** A 4-word packet costs about 98 ns, 24.6 ns per word, so the cost is per
  packet.
- **Instruction bytes do not track time across channels.** At N = 16,384 the 4-word arm carries
  36x fewer instruction bytes (10,864 against 393,444) but is only 2.5x faster.
- **Unexplained:** whether the ~95 ns per packet is the shim BD repeat, the stream or the tile's
  control port. This sitting does not separate them.

**What it means for the engine** (DERIVED, not measured on the engine):
- **BD rewrites gain nothing.** A shim or MemTile BD is 8 words, so as control packets it is two
  4-word packets, about 196 ns. That is no better than the ~145 ns per op the cost model priced
  for appended BD writes.
- **The cheaper half of AMD's mechanism is the other one:** cores writing their own tile DMAs
  with `st.tm`, a core instruction rather than any DDR-borne packet. The engine's per-round
  packets are shim and MemTile tasks, which no core can reach with `st.tm`, so that is a design
  question, not a port.
- **Not tested:** whether control packets can be pipelined so their cost overlaps compute. That
  would change the conclusion, and a dispatch-time slope cannot show it.

**Two findings from building it** (each observed once):
- **One control packet per stream packet.** All control packets sent inside one stream packet
  timed out at N = 4: the control port took the first one only, so the lock release never
  arrived. That matches the upstream test's one-transfer-per-write shape. The same writes, one
  stream packet each, were exact.
- **A first sweep stopped on its first design** with an ERT timeout. My design released lock 1
  on every run with nothing to acquire it, and the lock saturates. One `write32` resetting it per
  dispatch, identical in every arm, fixed it: 300 consecutive exact runs. The amendment was
  recorded before any timing was read.

Logs:
- [ctrl_packet_vs_write32_phoenix_desktop2_20261013T025614Z.log](../results/aie/ctrl_packet_vs_write32_phoenix_desktop2_20261013T025614Z.log), the sweep;
- [ctrl_packet_vs_write32_phoenix_desktop2_20261013T025452Z.log](../results/aie/ctrl_packet_vs_write32_phoenix_desktop2_20261013T025452Z.log), the stopped first sweep, with no timing.

## AMD's own stack runs YOLOv8s 19% faster with one compiler option its default leaves off: `enable_cost_model_tiling` (2026-10-13, Desktop 2)

**Question.** AMD's compiled xmodel records 119 compile options
([census](#what-amds-compiled-yolov8-runs-its-control-barely-grows-while-its-work-doubles-2026-10-13-desktop-2)),
and several that sound like speed levers are off in Ryzen AI 1.7.1's default X1 config. Does
turning one on make AMD's YOLOv8s faster at identical output?

**How the options were set.** The EP's `config_file` provider option takes a config file.
`tools/amd_xcompiler_config.py` writes one from the config the EP itself recorded in a compiled
cache (`context.json`). It sets each override in both places the EP keeps `xcompilerAttrs`: the
X1 target and the `fuse_DPU` pass. `tools/amd_vitisai_yolo.py` gained `--config-file` and
`--dump-heads`. Each arm compiled into its own fresh cache.

Three checks per arm:
- **Did the option reach the compiler?** The xmodel's root attribute must move
  (`amd_xmodel_census.py --root-attrs`).
- **Did placement change?** `context.json` must still list 922 nodes in one DPU subgraph. With a
  `config_file`, the EP writes no `vitisai_ep_report.json`.
- **Did the output change?** The raw heads must match the control's bit for bit.

**The control.** The EP's own config passed unchanged as `config_file` reproduces the default
build exactly: all 119 root attributes and the `mc_code` sha256 `2171462474654362`. So the
`config_file` path itself changes nothing.

**Smoke, 20 frames per arm** (screening only):

| option set to true | root attribute | `mc_code` | placement | heads vs control |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `enable_weights_prefetch` | 0 → 1 | byte-identical | 922 / 1 | identical |
| `enable_ifm_stationary` | 0 → 1 | byte-identical | 922 / 1 | identical |
| `enable_weights_stationary` | 0 → 1 | byte-identical | 922 / 1 | identical |
| `enable_cost_model_tiling` | 0 → 1 | **106,168 → 119,676 B** | 922 / 1 | identical |

The first three reach the compiler but leave the compiled program byte-identical, so on YOLOv8s
they change nothing that runs. They were not timed.

**The sitting** (pre-registered, scratch sha256 `9c7c7dce...`). `amd_vitisai_yolo.py` ran on
`bus.jpg`, 50 warm-up and 500 timed frames per run, in the order control, option, option,
control. Each run was its own process, with `xrt-smi` idle before it, under
`research-lowlevel --npu` (`timing_eligible: true`, no foreign context).

| arm | `session.run` ms | G2G ms |
|---|---:|---:|
| control (AMD default) | 13.273 / 13.235 | 17.146 / 17.100 |
| `enable_cost_model_tiling` | **10.697 / 10.738** | **14.513 / 14.572** |

- **Gate X: passes.** All four runs' last-frame heads are bit-identical (max abs diff 0 over 6
  outputs).
- **W: passes.** The option is faster in every pairing.
- **Effect:** −2.537 ms of `session.run` (0.809x, −19.1%) and −2.581 ms G2G (MEASURED).

**What changed underneath** (static declarations, census):
- `mc_code` grew 106,168 → 119,676 B, and its `0x0B`-headed words 1,757 → 1,772.
- **Declared traffic barely moved:** weight reads 87.9 → 82.7 MB, activation reads 138.1 → 144.3
  MB, writes 73.0 → 73.4 MB, a total of 299.0 → 300.4 MB (subgraph-level fields; see the
  basis caveat in the census section).
- **So AMD's time is not set by its declared bytes.** 19% less time for 0.5% more declared
  traffic answers the bytes-or-compute question the census left open, on the bytes side.
- **Unexplained here:** what the cost-model tiler chose differently. Decoded
  [below](#what-the-cost-model-tiler-changes-and-where-its-23-ms-comes-from-2026-10-13-desktop-2), with per-layer device timings.

**What it means for the comparisons in this file.**
- **AMD's default is not AMD's best.** Every AMD figure on this page used the EP's default config,
  and each stays correct for that config.
- **On YOLOv8s, AMD's best known G2G is now 14.54 ms** (this sitting). The engine's merged YOLOv8s
  read 17.20 ms in the Block 3 sitting. That was a different sitting, so the two are not compared
  here as one result, but the gap the engine has to close is larger than it was.
- **Untested:** other models beyond YOLOv8n ([below](#on-yolov8n-the-option-buys-94-and-the-engine-keeps-its-lead-from-the-host-side-only-2026-10-13-desktop-2)), and energy.
- **Whether future AMD arms should run with it** is a methodology decision, recorded here and not
  taken.

Log: [amd_cost_model_tiling_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T030644Z.log](../results/aie/amd_cost_model_tiling_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T030644Z.log).

### On YOLOv8n the option buys 9.4%, and the engine keeps its lead, from the host side only (2026-10-13, Desktop 2)

**Setup.** This is the same method as the YOLOv8s sitting above, pre-registered (scratch sha256
`5b5d4a57...`, with an amendment recorded before any run).
- **The two AMD arms:** the EP's own config (root attributes equal to the default build's) and the
  same config plus `enable_cost_model_tiling`. The option moved the root attribute 0 → 1 and grew
  `mc_code` from 93,840 to 99,820 B. Both arms run with 922 nodes in one DPU subgraph.
- **A third arm:** the engine's merged YOLOv8n container with `--silu-sigmoid`, from the
  [Block 3 sitting](#with-the-shipped-silu-recipe-ptr-does-not-carry-yolov8s-past-amds-stack-1720-against-1706-ms-2026-10-13-desktop-2).
- **Order and method:** AMD default, AMD option, engine, engine, AMD option, AMD default. Each run
  is 50 + 500 frames on `bus.jpg` in its own process, with `xrt-smi` idle before it
  (`timing_eligible: true`, no foreign context).

| arm | G2G ms | `session.run` / dispatch ms | host-side ms |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| AMD default | 10.749 / 10.799 | 6.930 / 6.937 | letterbox 1.82, decode+NMS 2.00-2.03 |
| AMD + `enable_cost_model_tiling` | 10.094 / 10.141 | 6.271 / 6.288 | letterbox 1.81-1.84, decode+NMS 2.01 |
| engine (merged, `--silu-sigmoid`) | **8.206 / 8.212** | 7.306 / 7.320 (+ 0.41-0.43 readback) | preprocess 0.31, decode+NMS 0.16 |

- **Gate X: passes.** The option arm's heads are bit-identical to the default arm's in all four AMD
  runs.
- **W: passes.** The option is faster in every pairing: −0.654 ms of `session.run` (0.906x,
  −9.4%) and −0.657 ms G2G. That is half its YOLOv8s effect in relative terms.
- **L (the engine keeps its lead): passes.** The engine's G2G is below the option arm's in all four
  pairings: 8.21 against 10.12 ms, 1.23x.

**Where the lead comes from.** The engine's dispatch alone (7.31 ms) is slower than AMD's whole
`session.run` with the option (6.28 ms). AMD's figure even includes its CPU quantize and
dequantize, so on the NPU side **AMD is already ahead on YOLOv8n** too.

The engine's lead is host-side:
- preprocessing 0.31 ms against a 1.82 ms letterbox;
- fused decode 0.16 ms against 2.01 ms.

A faster AMD host path would erase it.

**Correctness.** The engine arm returned 5.00 detections per frame. Its YOLOv8n container was not
verified layer by layer; only the YOLOv8s merged container was (66/66).

Logs:

- [amd_cost_model_tiling_yolov8n_desktop2_20261013T031617Z.log](../results/aie/amd_cost_model_tiling_yolov8n_desktop2_20261013T031617Z.log), a first attempt that stopped at the engine arm because I passed the container path relative to the wrong working directory. Its two AMD runs (10.719 / 10.068 ms G2G) are not used.

### What the cost-model tiler changes, and where its 2.3 ms comes from (2026-10-13, Desktop 2)

**Question.** The YOLOv8s section above left open what `enable_cost_model_tiling` does
differently. Declared traffic barely moved, so where does the 19% come from?

**1. Static decode: per-layer re-read factors.** All factors here use AMD's per-layer records.
Its subgraph-level byte fields are exactly 2x their sum in all four xmodels, while the op counts
agree 1x. Two candidates, neither ruled out:
- the subgraph counts each byte over two hops (DDR to MemTile, then MemTile to core);
- the subgraph roll-up duplicates the records.

The per-layer level is the one whose numbers match tensor sizes. `model.0`'s 1,700,352 B input is
a channel-padded 640×640 plus halo. That makes it the plausible per-frame level; it is a check,
not a verdict.

The decode itself: `tools/amd_xmodel_census.py --layers` prints
every per-layer record in AMD's compiled program. `tools/amd_layer_tiling_diff.py` joins each
convolution to its ONNX node. It then divides the declared bytes by the size of the tensor they
move, which gives a weight re-read factor `w_rr` and an input re-read factor `i_rr`. Its join
check holds on all 71 convolutions of each model: the declared op count equals the ONNX conv's
exactly, or half of it for a merged `Split` half. That count is also identical between the two
arms. Both models, both arms:
- **AMD's default reads nearly every convolution's weights about 4 times.** `w_rr` is 4.1–4.3
  on 68 of 71 layers, in both YOLOv8s and YOLOv8n. Four is the number of reachable columns
  ([SILICON](SILICON.md)), so the likely reading is that each column fetches the whole weight
  tensor and the columns split the image. That reading is DERIVED; it was not observed.
- **The option changes the split on a few layers, not everywhere.** On YOLOv8s, 10 layers change
  their weight re-read class; on YOLOv8n, 3. For example, the four 256-channel 20×20 bottleneck
  convolutions go from `w_rr` 4.2 / `i_rr` 3.4 to `w_rr` 2.0 / `i_rr` 6.2. On most of the other
  layers the factors shift by a few percent.
- **The tiler minimizes neither bytes nor padded work.** On YOLOv8s, `w_rr` falls on 54 layers
  and rises on 6, and `i_rr` rises on 35. Array utilization (`workload / workload_on_arch`) rises
  on 7 layers and falls on 7.

**2. AMD's own per-layer device timestamps.** The xcompiler attribute `profile` (uint 1) adds
about 720 B of `mc_code`. With `DEEPHI_PROFILING=1` set, XRT then writes two files: per-layer
start and end events, and their timer cycles. `tools/amd_dpu_layer_profile.py` parses them. Of
109 layer records, 89 are timestamped per frame.

**The sitting** (pre-registered, scratch sha256 `9405c2b4...`). Both arms were compiled with
`profile=1`: the default config, and the default plus the option. Order: default, option,
option, default. Each run was 5 warm-up + 50 timed frames in its own process, with `xrt-smi`
idle before it (`timing_eligible: true`).

| gate | criterion | result |
|---|---|---|
| H | heads bit-identical across the 4 runs and to the unprofiled default build | **pass** (max diff 0) |
| R | each arm's two frame-span medians within 2% | **pass** (0.53%, 1.34%) |
| T (a check, not blind) | timer unit: the span at 1.80 GHz is below `session.run`, and at the header's declared 1000 MHz it is above | **pass** (12.15 ms < 13.20 ms < 21.87 ms) |
| A | per-layer deltas sum to within 20% of the frame-span delta | **pass** (101.9%) |

- **The timer runs at the core clock.** The record header declares 1000 MHz, which would make
  the device span longer than the whole `session.run`. Gate T was written after a smoke run had
  shown a 22.4M-cycle span, so it is a check, and it only bounds the clock from below: anything
  above about 1.66 GHz passes, and the 1.6 GHz nameplate figure fails.
- **What pins 1.80 GHz is the delta.** The span falls by 4.18M cycles, which at the measured
  1.80 GHz core clock ([SILICON](SILICON.md)) is 2.32 ms, against a 2.30 ms `session.run` drop in
  the same sitting, within 1%. This section converts at 1.80 GHz (DERIVED). The remaining
  1.05 ms of `session.run` (13.20 − 12.15) fits the CPU quantize and dequantize inside it, but it
  is not measured.
- **The profiled sitting reproduces the effect.** At 1.80 GHz the device span falls 12.15 →
  9.83 ms (−2.32 ms). In the same sitting `session.run` fell 13.20 → 10.90 ms (−2.30 ms).
- **Instrumentation does not change the outcome:** the profiled builds' `session.run` (13.32 /
  13.08 and 10.84 / 10.97 ms) is within 0.2 ms of the unprofiled sitting above.

**Where the 2.32 ms comes from:**

| layers (by conv input size) | default ms | option ms |
|---|---:|---:|
| conv, 20×20 (18) | 2.395 | 1.746 |
| conv, 40×40 (25) | 3.657 | 2.750 |
| conv, 80×80 (20) | 3.059 | 2.464 |
| conv, 160×160 (6) | 0.867 | 0.802 |
| conv, 320×320 (1) | 0.380 | 0.213 |
| conv, 640×640 (1) | 0.169 | 0.169 |
| transpose, eltwise, pool, upsample (18) | 1.512 | 1.531 |

- **Only convolutions get faster.** 73 layers are faster and 16 slower; the gains sum to
  2.437 ms and the losses to 0.074 ms. Non-convolution layers are unchanged (+0.02 ms). The gap
  between layers grows by 0.04 ms.
- **The largest single gain is `model.7`,** the stride-2 3×3 convolution from 256 to 512
  channels. It goes from 0.757 to 0.345 ms, 17% of the whole gain. Its declared input re-read
  falls from 10.9× to 4.6×, and its utilization rises from 0.625 to 1.0.
- **The four 20×20 bottleneck convolutions** each save 0.08–0.10 ms. They trade weight re-reads
  for input re-reads (above), and their utilization rises from 0.625 to 0.833.
- **Unexplained.** `model.1` and `model.3` get faster (−0.17 and −0.06 ms) although their
  declared bytes rise and their utilization falls (1.0 → 0.75 and 0.625). Neither declared
  traffic nor utilization predicts their gain. How the columns overlap DMA with compute is not
  in the static record.

**3. Set against the engine (Block 5 input).** The same tool reads the engine's merged
container. Per layer, the engine's activation packets (6,400 B each, with halo and channel
padding) divided by the input tensor give the engine's input re-read factor (DERIVED):

| conv input bytes per frame (MB) | AMD default | AMD option | engine |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| YOLOv8s | 57.9 | 61.0 | 236.4 |
| YOLOv8n | 26.7 | 28.4 | 82.5 |

- **The engine reads each convolution's input far more often:** 3.9 times as often as AMD's
  option arm on YOLOv8s, and 2.9 times on YOLOv8n.
- **Corrected figure.** A first version of this analysis
  ([amd_tiling_decode_yolov8s_n_desktop2_20261013T034053Z.log](../results/aie/amd_tiling_decode_yolov8s_n_desktop2_20261013T034053Z.log)) counted the engine's 8 C2f `cv1` convolutions twice, once
  per AMD `Split` half. It read 279.0 / 93.9 MB and 4.6x / 3.3x, which is superseded. AMD's own
  rows were right, because each half declares its own bytes. The per-resolution medians did not
  move.
- **The gap is widest at 20×20.** There, the engine's median `i_rr` is 16 on YOLOv8s against
  AMD's 1.7, and 8 against 1.0–1.1 on YOLOv8n.
- **This sizes the "fewer packets" lever, but it does not show it costs time.** The engine's
  YOLOv8s frame is instruction-stream bound, and how much of its time its packet count sets is
  not measured here. The manifest does not size the engine's weight reads per layer, so no
  engine `w_rr` is given.
- **What it does give Block 5:** a per-layer list of where the engine re-reads activations most,
  and AMD's own per-layer timings to compare a re-tiled engine layer against.

- [amd_tiling_decode_corrected_yolov8s_n_desktop2_20261013T041500Z.log](../results/aie/amd_tiling_decode_corrected_yolov8s_n_desktop2_20261013T041500Z.log), the static decode with the engine counted once per node, the

### The engine's YOLOv8s, layer by layer, against AMD's (2026-10-13, Desktop 2)

**Question.** AMD's per-layer device times are measured above. Where does the engine's YOLOv8s
NPU time go, layer by layer, and how does each convolution compare with AMD's?

**Method.** `tools/engine_layer_timing.py` times one layer at a time.
- **How it splits the stream.** It lowers the container's ONNX again and refuses unless that
  reproduces the container's workspace and every weight-packet byte. It then cuts `insts.bin`
  at each layer barrier, using each layer's task count. The emitter retires every task at a
  barrier, so the 66 pieces add up byte for byte to the 969,812 B stream.
- **How it times.** Each piece, the whole stream and an empty stream (header only) get one
  pre-built XRT run, the same start/wait path `GraphSession.dispatch` uses. One round is the
  whole stream, then every layer in order, then five empty dispatches, all on one staged frame.
- **The NOP copy.** `--nop` repeats all of this on a copy whose weight packets are NOP. That
  copy moves the same data and skips the arithmetic, so real minus NOP is a layer's core
  compute.

A layer's time is its dispatch median less the empty-dispatch median (DERIVED: this assumes
every dispatch pays the empty one's fixed cost once).

**The sitting** (pre-registered, scratch sha256 `605c89c3...`). The container is
`yolov8s_merged_silu`, main's engine with `--silu-sigmoid`. Two back-to-back invocations, each
real then NOP, 10 warm-up + 200 rounds.
- **A first attempt was not usable.** It read `timing_eligible: false`. The runner saw an NPU
  context it did not own, because it never saw the Python process that Git Bash launched (its
  tree peaked at 10.9 MB). The context's PID changed exactly at the run boundary, which
  suggests it was this tool's own process, but that is not established.
- **The rerun.** I launched Python directly, logged an amendment before running it, and the
  runner then owned every context (`timing_eligible: true`).

| gate | criterion | result |
|---|---|---|
| E | heads after the per-layer sequence equal to the whole stream's, every round | **pass**: 0 mismatches in 840 rounds (both arms, both runs) |
| C | net layer times sum to within 10% of the whole stream less one empty dispatch | **pass**: 103.7–104.7% |
| R | each arm's whole-stream medians in the two runs within 2% | **pass**: 16.144 / 16.136 ms real, 12.289 / 12.278 ms NOP |

- **The fixed cost per dispatch:** the empty dispatch costs 0.096–0.100 ms.
- **The split is exact.** The per-layer sequence produces the same heads as the whole stream,
  so the layer times describe the same computation.

**Engine against AMD, the 63 convolutions** (AMD's two `Split` halves summed per node; the engine's 3
MaxPools take 0.18 ms more):

| conv input | n | engine | engine NOP | engine compute | AMD default | AMD + option | engine / AMD option |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 640×640 | 1 | 0.597 | 0.414 | 0.183 | 0.169 | 0.169 | 3.53x |
| 320×320 | 1 | 0.796 | 0.587 | 0.209 | 0.380 | 0.213 | 3.73x |
| 160×160 | 5 | 1.849 | 1.361 | 0.488 | 0.867 | 0.802 | 2.30x |
| 80×80 | 18 | 5.597 | 4.183 | 1.414 | 3.059 | 2.464 | 2.27x |
| 40×40 | 22 | 5.143 | 4.045 | 1.098 | 3.657 | 2.750 | 1.87x |
| 20×20 | 16 | 2.505 | 2.002 | 0.503 | 2.395 | 1.746 | 1.44x |
| **all** | **63** | **16.488** | **12.593** | **3.895** | **10.527** | **8.144** | **2.02x** |

The scopes differ. The engine column is host-timed dispatches less a fixed cost; AMD's are device
timestamps at 1.80 GHz. Both are DERIVED, and the comparison is per layer, not per frame.

- **The engine's convolutions take twice AMD's best:** 16.49 ms against 8.14 ms. The engine is
  faster on only 4 of 63, all of them small.
- **The engine's arithmetic is not the problem.** Its core compute is 3.90 ms, less than half
  of AMD's entire convolution time. The other 12.59 ms is what the NOP copy also spends: moving
  activations and weights and running the tasks. On the median convolution that is 70% of the
  layer's time.
- **The gap is largest where the tensors are largest, not where the re-read factor is.** The
  three layers at 160×160 and above run 3.4–3.7x AMD. The 20×20 layers, where the engine re-reads
  its input 16 times against AMD's 1.7, run only 1.44x. Their tensors are small, so even 16x
  re-reads move little.
- **The ten largest gaps** are mostly 3×3 convolutions at 80×80 and above, plus 1×1
  convolutions over wide inputs (384 or 768 channels). On the 1×1s, real equals NOP to within
  0.02 ms, so they are pure data movement. The full list is in the analysis log.

**What sets the data-movement time (exploratory, not pre-registered).** A least-squares fit of
each layer's NOP time:
- **Activation packets alone explain most of it:** about 0.26 µs per 6,400 B packet plus 44 µs
  per layer, R² 0.94.
- **Rounds alone do not:** R² 0.28.

Every packet is the same size, so this cannot separate a per-packet cost from a byte-rate limit.
The earlier instruction-stream model also grows with packets. Which of the three sets the time is
unexplained.

Either way, packet count is the variable that tracks the engine's non-compute time. AMD's
re-read factors (above) show how many packets the same convolutions can be done with: 3.9x fewer
input bytes on YOLOv8s. That makes the high-resolution layers, not the 20×20 ones, the first
target for Block 5.

Logs:
- [engine_layer_timing_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T044249Z.log](../results/aie/engine_layer_timing_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T044249Z.log), the sitting;
- [engine_vs_amd_layer_times_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T045000Z.log](../results/aie/engine_vs_amd_layer_times_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T045000Z.log), the join, the per-resolution table, the ranked gaps and the fit;
- [engine_layer_timing_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T044118Z.log](../results/aie/engine_layer_timing_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T044118Z.log), the attempt the runner marked ineligible; its numbers are not used.

#### What sets a layer's time: activation packets, not instruction ops (exploratory, offline)

The per-layer sitting above makes it possible to separate two things that grow together over whole
frames: activation packets and the instruction stream. I re-split the same container's stream into its 66
layer pieces and counted each piece's ops and bytes. Across layers they correlate with packets at only 0.49,
so the two are separable here. Fit of each layer's NOP time ([log](../results/aie/engine_layer_cost_drivers_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T051500Z.log)):

| model | R² | rms |
|---|---:|---:|
| packets alone (0.264 µs each + 44 µs) | 0.943 | 34 µs |
| instruction ops or bytes alone | 0.414 | 109 µs |
| packets + ops (0.235 µs per packet, 0.09 µs per op) | 0.979 | 21 µs |

- **What a layer costs, outside its arithmetic, is the activation packets delivered to the cores.** It is not
  the length of the control stream that delivers them.
- **This narrows the whole-frame cost model.** That model's ~16 ns per instruction byte is still the right
  per-frame fit, but across layers it is packets that track time.
- **It is consistent with the activation ring result.** The ring cut DDR traffic 38%, but every core still
  received one packet per chunk per group. Its time rose with its instruction stream.
- **Still open:** whether the cost is per packet or per byte (every packet is 6,400 B), and which stage of
  the path (shim, MemTile, core DMA, lock handshake) sets it. *[Partly answered 2026-10-15 by the
  [shim budget](#where-the-control-frames-time-goes-seen-from-the-shim-activation-bytes-on-the-transport-bound-layers-the-memtile-filling-on-the-compute-heavy-ones-exploratory-offline-2026-10-15-desktop-2): on the transport-bound layers the shim's activation stream (the MemTile
  never pushes back), on the compute-heavy ones a stage below the MemTile. Per packet against per byte stays open.]*

**Lever sizes (DERIVED, at 0.235 µs per packet).** A layer's packet count is 4 × G × T × C:
- G = ceil(Cout / 32), the output-channel groups;
- T is the spatial quads;
- C is the input chunks.

A core holds partial sums for 32 output channels only, so each extra group re-reads the whole input. Of
37,136 packets per YOLOv8s frame, 34,984 belong to the 57 multi-chunk layers.

| change | packets saved | DERIVED ms |
|---|---:|---:|
| loop all groups in-core while an input packet stays resident (only possible when C = 1) | 340 | 0.08 |
| each input fetch serves 2 groups (64 output channels per core pass) | 17,492 | 4.10 (2.06 from inputs ≥ 80×80) |
| bound: every layer at AMD's input re-read | 28,641 | 6.72 |

**What blocks the 2-group change is core memory.** Each core uses 59,392 of 65,536 B (MODEL_ZOO), leaving
6,144 B. That is 16,000 B of partial sums, a 3,200 B scratch tile, two 9,472 B weight objects, and two each of
the 6,400 B activation and 3,200 B output objects, plus a 2 KB stack. A second group's partial sums need
12,800 B more.
- **To make room,** something has to give up double-buffering. For example, activation and output depth 1
  frees 9,600 B.
- **The two weight objects would then hold both groups' weights,** leaving none prefetching.

How much that lost overlap costs is unmeasured. It decides whether the 4.1 ms is reachable.

#### Block 5, phase 1: single-buffering the cores costs 2.70 ms, so the 2-group design is stopped (2026-10-13, Desktop 2)

**Question.** Serving 2 output groups per input fetch was sized above at 4.10 ms saved (DERIVED). It needs
12,800 B more core data memory than the 6,144 B free, which forces single-buffered core fifos. What does
single-buffering cost on its own?

**Method.** `compile_graph_container(core_depths=(w, a, o))` sets the core-side object counts of the weight,
activation and output fifos; the MemTile side stays at 2. It is new on branch `block5-two-groups`, recorded in
the manifest when not (2, 2, 2), and the offline tests cover its validation. Three YOLOv8s containers with
`--silu-sigmoid` were built:
- **`d222`:** the shipped depths, rebuilt as the control;
- **`d111`:** every core fifo at depth 1. This is the 2-group design's buffering, since its two weight objects
  would hold both groups' weights at once;
- **`d211`:** weights still double-buffered.

All three have the same instruction stream and weight packets. The generated MLIR shows the core-side
activation fifos at depth 1 in `d111` and `d211`.

**The sitting** (pre-registered, scratch sha256 `6386039c...`). `tools/engine_layer_timing.py` ran 10 warm-up
+ 100 rounds per container, in the order `d222`, `d111`, `d211`, `d211`, `d111`, `d222`. Each run was its own
Python process with `xrt-smi` idle before it (`timing_eligible: true`).

| container | whole stream ms (two runs) | vs `d222` |
|---|---:|---:|
| `d222` (shipped) | 16.142 / 16.153 | - |
| `d211` | 17.180 / 17.251 | +1.068 |
| `d111` | 18.770 / 18.930 | **+2.703** |

- **Gate X: passes.** The raw heads of `d111` and `d211` are byte-equal to `d222`'s.
- **Every per-layer sequence was exact:** 0 mismatches in 660 rounds.
- **Kill line K was "`d111` more than 2.0 ms slower", and it triggers.** The 2-group design is stopped.

**Per input resolution** (ms; the saving is the 2-group prediction at 0.235 µs per packet, DERIVED):

| conv input | `d111` penalty | `d211` penalty | predicted saving | net if the design paid `d111`'s penalty |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 640×640 | +0.079 | +0.064 | 0.000 | −0.079 |
| 320×320 | +0.201 | +0.146 | 0.240 | +0.039 |
| 160×160 | +0.435 | +0.226 | 0.420 | −0.014 |
| 80×80 | +0.854 | +0.350 | 1.396 | +0.543 |
| 40×40 | +0.954 | +0.238 | 1.385 | +0.431 |
| 20×20 | +0.422 | +0.049 | 0.662 | +0.239 |
| **all (incl. 3 pools)** | **+2.987** | **+1.077** | **4.104** | **+1.117** |

- **Overlap is worth about 3 ms.** With nothing double-buffered, the cores lose 2.7–3.0 ms of overlap between
  transfer and compute. Weights alone account for about two-thirds of it (`d111` against `d211`).
- **The design would net about 1.1 ms (DERIVED),** and only if it paid no more than `d111`'s penalty. Twice the
  arithmetic per held object would plausibly cost more overlap, not less. That is below the line set before the
  run, so phase 2 was not started.
- **On the highest-resolution layers it would gain nothing.** The 640, 320 and 160 inputs net −0.05 ms
  together, though they are where the engine trails AMD most. Their packets come from a single group (G = 1–2)
  and from over-read, which more output channels per pass cannot touch.
- **What would reopen it:** core memory that keeps the weights double-buffered, which the `d211` row prices at
  +1.08 ms. The arithmetic: 49,792 B after single-buffering activations and outputs, plus 12,800 B of partial
  sums, plus a third 9,472 B weight object, is 72,064 B against a 65,536 B core. It does not fit as laid out.

Log: [engine_core_depth_probe_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T053413Z.log](../results/aie/engine_core_depth_probe_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T053413Z.log),
the sitting. The per-resolution table is computed in its companion analysis log,
[engine_core_depth_penalty_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T055500Z.log](../results/aie/engine_core_depth_penalty_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T055500Z.log).

#### Block 5: what a different packet shape could save (sized offline, 2026-10-13)

**Question.** With the 2-group design stopped, the next candidate keeps 32-channel groups but carries less junk
per packet. How much is that worth?

**Method.** Offline sizing over the 63 YOLOv8s convolutions (log below). It assumes activation bytes are what
costs, at the fitted 0.235 µs per 6,400 B packet. That assumption is untested, because every packet today is
6,400 B. Each layer keeps today's 5×20 tile, chunks and groups. Three variants:
- **S** carries exactly the kernel's extent per core (k1 5×20, k3s1 7×22, k3s2 11×41 per 8-channel block);
- **Q** fetches each quad's extent once and splits it on chip, so the four stacked cores share their halo rows;
- **A** is AMD's declared input bytes for the same layer.

| layers | today | S (no slack) | Q (quad halo) | AMD |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| all 63 convs | 236.4 MB | 185.1 MB (−1.88 ms) | 172.3 MB (−2.35 ms) | 53.1 MB (−6.72 ms) |
| 7 stride-2 3×3 | 72.1 MB | 40.6 MB (−1.15 ms) | 37.9 MB (−1.25 ms) | 15.0 MB |
| 32 stride-1 3×3 | 65.0 MB | 46.8 MB (−0.67 ms) | 36.7 MB (−1.04 ms) | 17.7 MB |
| 24 1×1 | 99.3 MB | 97.7 MB (−0.06 ms) | 97.7 MB | 20.4 MB (−2.89 ms) |
| inputs ≥ 160×160 (7) | 47.5 MB | 29.2 MB (−0.67 ms) | 27.4 MB (−0.74 ms) | 13.9 MB |

All savings are DERIVED.

- **A different shape is worth at most about 2 ms on YOLOv8s.** Half of that is the seven stride-2
  convolutions, whose 16×50 packet carries an 11×41 need.
- **The 1×1 layers are out of its reach.** They are 99 MB and about 2.9 ms of the distance to AMD. They carry no
  halo, so their excess is entirely the once-per-32-channels re-read, the lever phase 1 closed.
- **There is a structural obstacle.** Every kind shares one activation object size, so a tighter k3s2 plane
  needs either a per-kind object (more core buffers, against 6,144 B free) or a size every kind can use. The
  2026-09-20 sweep priced every buildable size as a regression, but it priced them with the instruction-byte cost
  model, which the per-layer fit above does not support at layer level. So that rejection rests on a model now
  in question; it is not overturned.

**The question this raises before anything is built.** The fit's 0.235 µs per packet is about 27 GB/s across
the array, roughly 6.8 GB/s per column. That is close to one 32-bit stream at the 1.80 GHz core clock
(7.2 GB/s), and to the 7 GB/s the one-core MemTile hop probe measured (0.143 ms per MB). That suggests a
per-column ceiling: one shim-to-MemTile activation stream feeding four cores. This is DERIVED and untested.
- **If it holds,** the lever is more activation streams per column, not packet shape. Each column's second
  shim MM2S channel carries only weights, about 57 MB per frame against 237 MB of activations. *[83.6 MB, not ~57: 20.99 MB per column with the replay, from the schedule and the instruction stream ([shim budget](#where-the-control-frames-time-goes-seen-from-the-shim-activation-bytes-on-the-transport-bound-layers-the-memtile-filling-on-the-compute-heavy-ones-exploratory-offline-2026-10-15-desktop-2)), as the sizing section below already reads.]*
- **If the ceiling is per core instead,** shape and bytes are the lever and the sizing above applies.

A probe that drives one, two and four cores of one column from one shim channel, and four cores from two,
would decide which.

Log: [engine_packet_shape_sizing_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T061500Z.log](../results/aie/engine_packet_shape_sizing_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T061500Z.log).

#### The engine's activations are capped at one shim stream per column, and a second stream doubles the rate (2026-10-13, Desktop 2)

**Question.** The per-layer fit put the engine's data movement at about 27 GB/s, 6.8 GB/s per column. Is that
one shim-to-MemTile stream per column, or a per-core limit?

**Method.** `tools/stream_ceiling_probe.py` moves input only, in the engine's 6,400 B objects, through the
MemTile as the engine does, with no compute. It varies two things:
- how many cores one shim MM2S stream feeds: 1 (MemTile forward), 2 or 4 (MemTile split);
- whether a column's four cores are fed by one shim stream or by two.

It runs these on one column and on all four. There are 256 to 2,048 objects per core, 3 rotated rounds × 30
dispatches, and each measurement is its own process. The rate is 1 / slope of time against MB.

**The sitting** (pre-registered, scratch sha256 `3a6df6b4...`). A 5-iteration smoke run of four routes was
seen before the criteria were written, and the pre-registration says so. The sitting read `timing_eligible:
true`.

| route | cores | rate (MEASURED) | intercept |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| one shim stream → 1 core | 1 | 6.57 GB/s | 0.081 ms |
| one shim stream → 2 cores | 2 | 6.82 GB/s | 0.096 ms |
| one shim stream → 4 cores (the engine's layout) | 4 | 6.88 GB/s | 0.124 ms |
| two shim streams → 2 + 2 cores | 4 | **13.37 GB/s** | 0.083 ms |
| all 4 columns, one stream each | 16 | 27.17 GB/s | 0.172 ms |
| all 4 columns, two streams each | 16 | **50.36 GB/s** | 0.100 ms |

**Verdict: COLUMN.** The pre-registered test needed both parts:
- **Four cores on one stream are no faster than one:** 1.05x, against a limit of ≤ 1.25x.
- **A second stream nearly doubles a column:** 1.94x, against a requirement of ≥ 1.6x.

The four columns are independent (3.95x one column).

**Checks.**
- **Time is linear in volume on every route** ([per-volume points](../results/aie/stream_ceiling_points_phoenix_desktop2_20261013T063000Z.log)), up to 52 MB per channel. A truncated
  descriptor would show as large volumes finishing too fast.
- **The shim can only complete once the cores have taken all but a few objects,** so the bytes arrived.
- **The 50.36 GB/s read rate on eight channels contradicts** the 26–28 GB/s shared cap that
  [SILICON 1.6](SILICON.md) inferred from GroupNorm and memcpy. That inference is now marked there as not holding
  for reads alone. Both earlier readings were confounded by concurrent writes or limited to four channels each
  way.

**What this explains.**
- **The engine runs at the ceiling.** The single-stream rate is close to one 32-bit stream at the 1.80 GHz core
  clock (7.2 GB/s, DERIVED). The engine's fitted 0.235 µs per 6,400 B packet is 27.2 GB/s, the same as the
  all-columns, one-stream route. So the engine's YOLOv8s activation transport runs at this ceiling (the match is
  DERIVED; the ceiling is MEASURED).
- **It explains why earlier transport experiments could not win.** The MemTile hop costs nothing, the ring and
  the weight buffer moved bytes around the same single stream, and packet shape only trims bytes on it.
- **The lever is a second stream per column.** Today each column's second shim MM2S channel carries only
  weights: about 57 MB per YOLOv8s frame (29.5 MB of packets plus the stride-0 replay) *[83.6 MB, not ~57: 20.99 MB per column with the replay, from the schedule and the instruction stream ([shim budget](#where-the-control-frames-time-goes-seen-from-the-shim-activation-bytes-on-the-transport-bound-layers-the-memtile-filling-on-the-compute-heavy-ones-exploratory-offline-2026-10-15-desktop-2)), as the sizing section below already reads.]*, against 237 MB of
  activations.

At the measured rates, the activations alone take about 8.7 ms per frame at 27.17 GB/s and about 4.7 ms at
50.36 GB/s. That is up to ~4 ms (DERIVED), if the weights can share the streams without their own channel.
How to carry them is the open design question.

Log: [stream_ceiling_phoenix_desktop2_20261013T060213Z.log](../results/aie/stream_ceiling_phoenix_desktop2_20261013T060213Z.log).

#### Block 5: what letting weights share the second stream could save (sized offline, 2026-10-13)

**Question.** Each column has two shim MM2S streams, one carrying only activations and one only weights. If both
streams could carry a mix, how much faster would YOLOv8s's data movement get, and which designs reach how much
of that?

**Model.** The YOLOv8s schedule was lowered again from the container, giving each layer's activation and weight
bytes per column: 237.7 MB and 83.6 MB per frame, plus 27.8 MB of drains on the other direction. Each layer's
transport time is taken as the busier channel's bytes in the slowest column at 6.88 GB/s per stream, the probe's
rate. Against the measured per-layer NOP times this model fits R² 0.941 with slope 1.138, so it explains the
engine's data-movement time. Savings below are scaled by that slope; all are DERIVED.

| design | per-layer channel use | modelled transport | saving |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| today | activations on stream 0, weights on stream 1 | 8.673 ms | - |
| two halves, static | cores 0–1's activations on stream 0, cores 2–3's and all weights on stream 1 | 7.389 ms | 1.46 ms |
| per-layer quarters | weights plus the activations of k of 4 cores on stream 1, k chosen per layer | 6.402 ms | 2.59 ms |
| ideal balance | both streams carry any mix | 5.863 ms | 3.20 ms |

- **Packet order bounds what is reachable.** A core must receive its packets in order. Within a layer, each core's
  activations and all of a column's weights therefore have to stay on one stream, which rules out the ideal.
  Per-layer quarters keep that order and reach 81% of the ideal. Choosing halves per layer gains nothing over the
  static split.
- **What it takes to build:** packet-switched routes. In this mlir-aie, that means `PacketFlow` with explicit
  tile DMA programs, buffers and locks, after upstream's `packet_switch` example, since `ObjectFifo` does not
  route by packet ID.
  - **What changes:** the transport in `design.py`, and the emitter stamping a packet ID on each shim task and
    picking its stream.
  - **What does not change:** the core kernel `engine.cc`.
- **The cost risk is task count** (answered in the next subsection: splitting by core costs ~2.0 ms, alternating whole quads does not). Today a fill carries about four packets, set by the quad object. If carrying
  some cores' packets on another stream splits fills, each extra 1,000 tasks costs about 0.37 ms (the per-layer
  fit's 0.09 µs per op, 4 ops per task, DERIVED). A full doubling would erase the quarters' gain. Whether fills
  can stay at four packets with 1- or 2-packet objects is unchecked.
- **Packet mode itself is unmeasured.** It is untested whether a stream keeps its ~6.9 GB/s with packet headers
  and two sources merging at one destination.

Before any engine work, the stream ceiling probe can add a packet-switched route: two shim streams each carrying
mixed packet IDs to a MemTile split and to the cores. It would measure that rate directly.

Log: [engine_stream_sharing_sizing_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T070000Z.log](../results/aie/engine_stream_sharing_sizing_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T070000Z.log).

#### Block 5: alternating whole quads between a column's two streams runs at full rate in packet mode, and nets 0.6-1.9 ms on YOLOv8s (2026-10-13, Desktop 2)

**Question.** The sizing above left two risks: extra shim tasks, and whether a stream keeps its rate in packet
mode. Both are answered here. Task counts are offline and DERIVED; the transport is a pre-registered sitting
(MEASURED).

**Splitting a fill by core is too expensive.** YOLOv8s issues 5,509 activation tasks per frame, 6.74 objects
each; 4,774 of them carry a single quad, meaning one 6,400 B object for each of the four cores. Every such task
would become two, adding +5,621 tasks, about 2.02 ms at 0.36 µs per task (4 instruction ops at the per-layer
fit's 0.09 µs).
- Static halves would then net −0.56 ms.
- Per-layer quarters would net +0.57 ms, and about zero once the array-wide cap below is applied.

**Alternating whole quads instead.** Each quad goes to one stream or the other by its position in the column's
quad sequence, and lands in one of two MemTile buffers. Each core's MemTile output reads the two buffers in the
same fixed pattern, so every core still receives its packets in order. Only multi-quad fills split: +783 tasks
for 1-in-2 alternation, +1,116 for a per-layer ratio.

**The transport, measured** ([tools/stream_share_probe.py](../tools/stream_share_probe.py), pre-registered
scratch sha256 `3fe02faf...` before any run of the tool; a hang-only smoke of the four routes ran after the
hash, as the pre-registration declared). The setup:
- Engine object sizes, no compute.
- Per round and column: 4 quads plus 4 weight objects, 37,888 B. That is a weight-to-activation ratio of 0.37,
  against YOLOv8s's 0.35.
- `base` is today's layout: stream 0 carries the quads, stream 1 broadcasts the weights.
- `alt` sends quads 0 and 2 on stream 0. Stream 1, in packet mode, carries the weights as one packet fanned out
  to the four cores, then quads 1 and 3 as one packet each into the MemTile's second input.

The sitting was `timing_eligible: true` with no foreign context, at 3 rounds × 30 dispatches and 64–256 rounds
per dispatch:

| route | µs per round (fit) | busier stream | alt/base, fit | alt/base by per-volume minima |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| base | 15.376 | 6.66 GB/s | | |
| alt | 13.000 | 6.85 GB/s | **0.846** | 0.880–0.888 |
| base4 (all columns) | 16.384 | 6.25 GB/s | | |
| alt4 (all columns) | 14.388 | 6.19 GB/s | **0.878** | 0.876–0.891 |

**Verdict: GO.** All three pre-registered criteria hold:
- **Q1:** the packet-mode stream runs at 6.85 GB/s, against a bar of ≥ 6.19.
- **Q2:** alt/base is 0.846, against a bar of ≤ 0.92.
- **Q3:** the four-column ratio is 0.878, against a bar of ≤ 0.95.

The prediction at one stream's rate was 0.870. Packet headers, the weight fan-out and the alternating MemTile
chains cost nothing measurable.

The array-wide cap is present, though. At four columns every stream slows: base 6.66 → 6.25 GB/s (−6%) and
alt 6.85 → 6.19 GB/s (−10%), the same few-percent cap the stream-ceiling probe saw (50.36 vs 2 × 27.17).
The ratio survives because both routes pay it. The engine runs all four columns, where alt's packet-mode
stream reads 6.19 GB/s, exactly Q1's bar.

The alt fit is noisier: residuals reach ±117 µs, against ≤ 49 µs on the other routes, and its 128-round point
has a wide spread across rounds. The per-volume minima are tight, and the verdict holds by fit, by medians and by
minima ([points](../results/aie/stream_share_points_phoenix_desktop2_20261013T0915Z.log)). The source of the
noise is unexplained.

**Packet order forces one more rule, and sets the design.** A core consumes chunk by chunk: a weight packet,
then that chunk's activation object, with weights 2 deep. On a shared stream, a weight task running ahead of
the quads behind it deadlocks once the cores' weight buffer is full. YOLOv8s's weight tasks are long:
- 362 of 389 carry more than 2 packets, and the longest carry 128;
- 208 replay one run once per round, as an outer stride-0 dimension spanning rounds. The log's first
  section counts 352, because it includes any zero stride.

Two fixes don't fit:
- Splitting every run per chunk would add +8,422 tasks, about 3.0 ms.
- A MemTile FIFO for the longest run would need 1.18 MB against the MemTile's 512 KiB.

The arrangement that fits: per round, stream 1 sends its quads first, into buffer B, then the round's weights.
- Buffer B must hold one round's stream-1 quads. At 1-in-2 that is up to 16 quads (400 KiB).
- Replayed weight tasks become one per round, +864 tasks.
- 22 weight tasks that serve past their round need splitting.

**Net on YOLOv8s (DERIVED)**:
- **Static 1-in-2 alternation:** anchored on the measured four-column ratio, 0.878 × 8.673 ms modelled transport
  saves 1.20 ms. Its tasks (+783 + 864 + 22) cost 0.60 ms, which nets **0.60 ms**. That is marginal, and close
  to sitting-to-sitting noise.
- **Per-layer ratio: about 1.3 ms realistic, 1.85 ms upper bound.** q of every 4 quads goes on stream 1, chosen
  per layer under buffer B's limit. The best is q = 1 on 62 layers and q = 2 on 4, with 5 changes between
  layers. Its largest round fits in 8 slots, so the limit never binds.
  - **Uncapped:** the model saves 2.59 ms against +2,002 tasks (0.73 ms), which nets 1.85 ms.
  - **With the cap:** q = 1 loads all eight streams nearly evenly, the regime where the cap measured above
    binds (50.36 GB/s rather than 2 × 27.17). Scaling for it leaves about **1.3 ms**, the figure the
    measurements support. *[Superseded the same day by the measured q = 1 ratio: about 1.07 ms, in the next subsection.]*
- **Not measured:**
  - the q = 1 mix;
  - the quads-first order;
  - the deep buffer B;
  - per-chunk weight and activation consumption.

  The probe sent weights first, and its cores took all four weights before any activation.

**What building it takes.**
- **`design.py`:** each column's activation fifo becomes explicit MemTile DMA: two inputs, buffer A at 2 slots and
  buffer B at 8–16 slots via `BdIteration`, and per-core output chains in the period-4 pattern. The weights become
  a packet fan-out from stream 1. The core-side explicit buffer and lock pattern already exists in `design.py`
  (`_weight_buffer`, the activation ring). `engine.cc` is unchanged.
- **The emitter:**
  - assign quads to streams by position;
  - split multi-quad fills;
  - stamp packet IDs on stream-1 tasks;
  - reorder each round to quads-first, moving the `serves` await accounting with it;
  - split replayed weight tasks per round;
  - re-arm the MemTile pattern at the 5 changes of q.
- **First milestone, before any engine code:** an `alt_qf` variant of the probe with quads first, buffer B
  through iteration, cores consuming weight-activation pairs, and the q = 1 mix.

Logs:
- [sitting](../results/aie/stream_share_phoenix_desktop2_20261013T0900Z.log)
- [per-volume points](../results/aie/stream_share_points_phoenix_desktop2_20261013T0915Z.log)
- [task counts](../results/aie/engine_stream_split_tasks_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T080000Z.log)
- [packet order and per-layer ratio](../results/aie/engine_stream_share_order_yolov8s_desktop2_20261013T0930Z.log)

#### Block 5: the order the engine needs works too, and the per-layer design nets about 1.07 ms on YOLOv8s (2026-10-13, Desktop 2)

**Question.** The first stream-share sitting sent the weights first, and its cores took all four weights before
any activation. The engine cannot use that order. Its cores consume chunk by chunk, and on a shared stream a long
weight run blocks the quads behind it. Does the order the engine would need still run at full rate, and what does
the per-layer 1-in-4 mix that YOLOv8s mostly wants measure?

**Method.** The order under test (`build_qf` in
[tools/stream_share_probe.py](../tools/stream_share_probe.py)):
- **Stream order:** per round, stream 1 sends its quads first, into an 8-slot buffer B, then the round's weight
  run as one fanned-out packet.
- **MemTile:** chains use `BdIteration`, so buffer depth costs no descriptors. Core k reads position p of every 4
  from the slot that position owns.
- **Cores:** they consume weight, activation, weight, activation, as `engine.cc` does.

Three routes, each also in an all-four-column form:
- `base_i`: today's layout, with per-chunk consumption.
- `qf2`: 1-in-2 alternation.
- `qf1`: 1 quad in 4 on stream 1.

Bytes per round are as in the first sitting. The criteria were pre-registered before any run of these routes
(scratch sha256 `a3ef04bc...`), and a completion-only smoke ran after the hash, as declared. The sitting was
`timing_eligible: true` with no foreign context, at 3 rounds × 30 dispatches and 64–256 rounds per dispatch.

| route | µs per round | busier stream | vs base_i (fit) | vs base_i (per-volume minima) | one-stream prediction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| base_i | 15.665 | 6.54 GB/s | | | |
| qf2 | 13.649 | 6.53 GB/s | **0.871** | 0.869–0.887 | 0.870 |
| qf1 | 12.101 | 6.35 GB/s | **0.772** | 0.755–0.783 | 0.750 |
| base_i_4 | 16.440 | 6.23 GB/s | | | |
| qf2_4 | 14.402 | 6.19 GB/s | **0.876** | 0.881–0.898 | 0.870 |
| qf1_4 | 13.446 | 5.71 GB/s | **0.818** | 0.786–0.802 | 0.750 |

**Verdict: BUILD.** Every route completed, so there is no deadlock with quads first. The three pre-registered
criteria hold:
- **Q1:** quads-first at 1-in-2 is 0.871, against a bar of ≤ 0.92. The order, the deep buffer B and per-chunk
  consumption cost nothing beyond the first sitting.
- **Q2:** `qf1` on one column is 0.772, against ≤ 0.82.
- **Q3:** `qf1` on four columns is 0.818, against ≤ 0.85.

The four-column `qf1` misses its 0.750 prediction by the array cap. Its two streams are nearly balanced (76,800
and 63,488 B per round), every stream slows to 5.71 GB/s, and the array moves 41.7 GB/s in all. That falls short
of the stream-ceiling probe's 50.36 GB/s for pure reads; which resource sets this lower total is unexplained.

**On YOLOv8s (DERIVED, the pre-registered formula):** the measured four-column ratio applied to the 8.673 ms
modelled transport, at slope 1.138, less the counted task cost:
- **Per-layer design** (q = 1 on 62 layers): (1 − 0.818) × 8.673 × 1.138 − 0.732 = **1.07 ms per frame**. This
  supersedes the 1.3 ms (cap-scaled model) and 1.85 ms (uncapped) estimates above.
- **Static 1-in-2:** **0.62 ms**.

**What is still not measured:**
- the per-task issue cost (the probe chains descriptors; the 0.36 µs per task is the per-layer fit's);
- YOLOv8s's per-layer mix, which varies around the probe's fixed 0.37 weight ratio;
- compute overlapping the transport.

Logs: [sitting](../results/aie/stream_share_qf_phoenix_desktop2_20261013T1000Z.log),
[per-volume points and the derived nets](../results/aie/stream_share_qf_points_phoenix_desktop2_20261013T1015Z.log).

#### Campaign anchor: YOLOv8s trails AMD's best by 5.68 ms on the device and 2.76 ms glass to glass; retiring every 3rd task wins 0.23 ms; a 1-quad task costs 0.40 us more than its bytes in a bigger task (2026-10-13, Desktop 2)

These three sittings open the low-level optimisation campaign. They measure the bar, the first emitter knob, and
the per-task cost every Block 5 sizing had borrowed from a fit.

Containers: main `744909b`, `--engine graph --silu-sigmoid`. YOLOv8s carries 969,812 instruction bytes, with
0 host layers. Arms in every sitting:
- `tools/bench_layout_ab.py --alternate --rounds 4`, which reverses the arm order on even rounds;
- 50 warm-up + 500 timed frames per run on `bus.jpg`, with `xrt-smi` idle before every run;
- AMD's default build, and AMD with `enable_cost_model_tiling` (`amd_cfg`);
- all under `research-lowlevel.sh --npu`.

Every sitting was `timing_eligible: true`, with no foreign context, and every engine run read 5.00 detections per
frame.

**The anchor.** All values are ms over 4 runs per arm. Engine "device" is dispatch; AMD's is `session.run`.

| model | arm | G2G | device |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| YOLOv8s | engine | 17.208–17.252 | 16.326–16.359 |
| YOLOv8s | AMD default | 16.898–17.004 | 13.099–13.159 |
| YOLOv8s | AMD `amd_cfg` | **14.407–14.506** | **10.622–10.687** |
| YOLOv8n | engine | **7.618–8.132** | 6.929–7.274 |
| YOLOv8n | AMD default | 10.932–11.577 | 6.463–6.915 |
| YOLOv8n | AMD `amd_cfg` | 10.072–10.831 | **5.854–6.263** |

- **YOLOv8s against AMD's best:** the engine trails by **5.68 ms on the device** and **2.76 ms glass to glass**
  (means). It is the campaign's target, and it reproduces cd3c996's 17.20 against 14.54 ms.
- **YOLOv8n:** the engine leads glass to glass by 2.52 ms and trails by 1.04 ms on the device. Its lead is all
  host side, as before.
- **YOLOv8n drift:** the YOLOv8n sitting stepped within itself. Engine rounds 1–2 dispatched in 6.93 ms and
  rounds 3–4 in 7.24–7.27, and AMD's arms moved the same way. Read it as a range, not one number.

**Retire cadence (YOLOv8s).** These three containers are byte-identical apart from the token cadence:
- rb2 is the anchor container, 969,812 instruction bytes;
- rb3 retires every 3rd task, 933,028 B;
- rb4 retires every 4th, 900,644 B.

Pre-registered before any run (scratch sha256 `5c4e2fff...`): a WIN must be lower in all 4 rounds on both
dispatch and G2G, by at least 0.10 ms.

| cadence | dispatch, 4 rounds | mean | G2G mean | vs rb2 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| rb2 (control) | 16.374 / 16.390 / 16.400 / 16.355 | 16.380 | 17.266 | |
| **rb3** | 16.155 / 16.130 / 16.151 / 16.153 | **16.147** | **17.043** | **−0.233 / −0.223 ms, lower 4/4: WIN** |
| rb4 | 16.419 / 16.448 / 16.458 / 16.437 | 16.441 | 17.342 | +0.061 / +0.076 ms, higher 4/4: worse |

- **AMD's arms in the same sitting:** default 17.173–17.689 G2G (`session.run` 13.141–13.236), `amd_cfg`
  14.555–15.295 G2G (10.640–10.702).
- **The control reproduces the anchor:** dispatch 16.36–16.40 against 16.33–16.36.

**Attribution.** The instruction-byte model (16.08 ns per byte, `f7e75ec`) predicted −0.59 ms for rb3 and
−1.11 ms for rb4, falling monotonically with the bytes removed. rb3 saved less than half its prediction, and rb4
removed 69,168 B and got slower. Bytes removed therefore do not set the cost of this class of instruction.
`f7e75ec`'s fit was cross-model and correlational; this is the first controlled test of it inside one model.

The U-curve now holds on three models: SESR M7's minimum is at 2, and YOLOv8n's and YOLOv8s's at 3. The
mechanism is **unexplained**. The default stays 2, because SESR M7 pays 0.65 ms at rb3 (see the cadence lock in
DECISIONS). Any rule that ships rb3 must carry SESR M7 and YOLOv8n in the same sitting. *[Superseded the same
day: the frame rule below (rb3 from 2,000 shim tasks per frame) shipped after a sitting that carried SESR M7,
YOLOv8n, YOLOv8n-pose and YOLOv8s; the default is no longer a flat 2.]*

**Per-task issue cost (`tools/task_issue_probe.py`).**

The probe's design:
- the engine's activation path: 4 columns, ObjectFifo split, fills only, with no weights and no drains;
- tasks of k contiguous quads, retired engine-style (a token every 2nd task, ≤ 4 pending per channel);
- the grid is k ∈ {1, 2, 4, 16, 64} × Q ∈ {512, 1024} quads per column;
- 3 rotated rounds × 30 dispatches, each in its own child process.

Pre-registered (sha256 `f24a76de...`): fit `ms = a + b·MB + c·tasks`; R² < 0.95 means c is reported as
unexplained. An attempt that crashed in argument parsing before any dispatch was fixed and re-run; it produced no
measurement.

| Q | k | tasks | MB | mean ms | vs k=64, same bytes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 512 | 1 | 2,048 | 52.4 | 3.030 | **+0.815 ms = +0.404 µs per extra task** |
| 512 | 2 | 1,024 | 52.4 | 2.094 | −0.121 |
| 512 | 4 / 16 / 64 | 512 / 128 / 32 | 52.4 | 2.196 / 2.151 / 2.215 | −0.019 / −0.064 / 0 |
| 1024 | 1 | 4,096 | 104.9 | 5.802 | **+1.698 ms = +0.421 µs per extra task** |
| 1024 | 2 | 2,048 | 104.9 | 4.125 | +0.021 |
| 1024 | 4 / 16 / 64 | 1,024 / 256 / 64 | 104.9 | 4.151 / 4.196 / 4.104 | +0.046 / +0.092 / 0 |

- **The plane fails its bar.** R² is 0.9476, so the fitted c (0.394 µs) is not used, per the pre-registration.
- **The shape is a step, not a slope.** Tasks of 2 or more quads are indistinguishable from 64-quad tasks at both
  volumes: −0.12 to +0.09 ms across 128–2,048 extra tasks, under 0.1 µs each. Single-quad tasks cost
  0.40–0.42 µs more each. Two independent volumes agree, so merging two 1-quad tasks into one 2-quad task saves
  0.82–0.91 µs.
- **A defect in the pre-registration:** its nonlinearity clause (k=1 residuals above 3× the median) could not
  fire as written. The plane absorbed the k=1 excess into c, so the k=1 residuals (143–329 µs) sit under the
  561 µs bar. The step above is read from the per-k table, which was not pre-registered.
- **The rate checks out:** b gives 28.4 GB/s across the array, 7.1 GB/s per column, consistent with the measured
  6.9 GB/s per-stream ceiling.
- **Mechanism unexplained:** why a 25.6 KB task falls behind its transfer while a 51.2 KB task does not.

**Consequences, all DERIVED:**
- **YOLOv8s's dominant task is the expensive one.** 4,774 of its 5,509 activation tasks carry 1 quad. If every
  one paired with a neighbour, the upper bound is about 2 ms. The achievable share is whatever an offline count of
  same-channel, same-tile neighbours says, and that count comes before any code. The probe's k=2 was contiguous;
  a paired engine fill would be strided.
- **The stream-sharing net becomes a range.** Its 1.07 ms used 0.36 µs per added task.
  - If the 2,002 added tasks are single-quad, the per-layer design nets about **0.96 ms** and static 1-in-2
    about **0.54 ms**, right at Phase 2's 0.5 ms kill line.
  - If they are 2 quads or more, it nets about 1.79 / 1.22 ms.

  Which of the two applies is settled offline before Phase 2 code.

Two YOLOv8n attempts ran under a foreign 12–15-core `llama-quantize.exe` and were flagged `timing_eligible:
false`. They are not used and not committed; the sitting above waited for 5 quiet minutes.
